name: Swift
title: Swift: the language of iPhone and Mac apps
intro: Swift is Apple's language for apps on the iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch and Apple TV. Apple released it in 2014 to replace Objective-C, and made it open source a year later, so it also runs on Linux and Windows. Swift is built to be safe: every variable has a type the compiler checks, a value that may be missing has to be marked as optional and unwrapped before use, and arrays check that you stay inside them. It is also quick to write, with types worked out for you and no semicolons. These lessons cover the language itself, the part that is the same whether you go on to build iPhone apps with SwiftUI or command-line tools. Every example is a whole file and shows exactly what it prints. To run one yourself, install Swift (it comes with Xcode on a Mac; for Linux and Windows see swift.org), save the example as main.swift, and type swiftc main.swift -o main and then ./main.

lessons.title: Your first program
lessons.summary: print, let and var, types and string interpolation.

sections.p: A Swift program can start straight away: statements at the top of main.swift run in order, with no main function to write. print prints its values and ends the line. Given several values, it puts a space between them.
sections.code:
print("Hello, squirrel!")
print("Nuts:", 42)

sections.p: let makes a constant, which can't be given a new value, and var a variable, which can. Swift prefers let, and the compiler even warns about a var that never changes. The type comes after a colon, but usually Swift works it out from the value: let nuts = 7 is an Int.
sections.code:
let name: String = "Hazel"
var nuts = 7
nuts = nuts + 3
// name = "Bob"   <- error: cannot assign to a 'let' constant
let hungry = nuts < 20
print(name)
print(nuts)
print(hungry)

sections.p: Inside a string, \(...) puts in the value of any expression. Strings can also be joined with +, and count gives the number of characters.
sections.code:
let name = "Hazel"
let nuts = 7
print("\(name) has \(nuts) nuts")
print("Next week: \(nuts * 2)")
print("Name length: \(name.count)")
print(name + " the squirrel")
sections.out:
Hazel has 7 nuts
Next week: 14
Name length: 5
Hazel the squirrel

sections.p: Int holds whole numbers and Double numbers with a fractional part. Dividing two Ints drops the remainder, which % gives you. Swift never mixes number types by itself: an Int and a Double can't be added until you convert one with Double(...) or Int(...).
sections.code:
let nuts = 17
let squirrels = 5
print(nuts / squirrels)
print(nuts % squirrels)
print(Double(nuts) / Double(squirrels))
let weight = 6.0
print(weight)
print(Int(weight) + 1)

practice.code:
var acorns = 4
acorns += 2
let tree = "oak"
print("\(acorns) from the \(tree)")
practice.why: Each \(...) is replaced by the value inside, and acorns is 6 after += 2.

practice.code:
print(7 / 2)
print(7.0 / 2)
practice.why: Int divided by Int drops the remainder. 7.0 is a Double, so the 2 next to it is treated as a Double too.

practice.q: What happens when you give a let constant a new value?
options: The program stops when it reaches that line
practice.why: A let can be set only once. The mistake is caught before the program runs.

lessons.title: Decisions and loops
lessons.summary: if, switch with ranges, for-in and while.

sections.p: if needs no brackets around its condition, but the braces around its body are required, even for one line. The condition must be a real Bool: Swift doesn't treat 0 or an empty string as false.

Swift's switch can match several values, a range like 3...9, or a condition with where. It doesn't fall through to the next case, so no break is needed. A switch must cover every possible value, which for an Int means ending with default.
sections.code:
func describe(_ nuts: Int) -> String {
    switch nuts {
    case 0:
        return "none"
    case 1, 2:
        return "a few"
    case 3...9:
        return "some"
    case let n where n > 100:
        return "too many to count"
    default:
        return "lots"
    }
}

print(describe(0))
print(describe(2))
print(describe(5))
print(describe(40))
print(describe(500))
sections.out:
none
a few
some
lots
too many to count

sections.p: 1...5 is a range from 1 to 5 with both ends included, and 0..<3 leaves out the end. for-in walks through a range or an array. stride(from:to:by:) counts in steps, including backwards. while loops as long as its condition holds.

practice.why: 1...4 includes both ends: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10.

practice.code:
let n = 7
switch n {
case 0..<5:
    print("small")
case 5..<10:
    print("medium")
default:
    print("large")
}
practice.why: 7 is in 5..<10. Swift runs only the matching case and doesn't fall through.

practice.q: How many times does  for i in 0..<4  run?
practice.why: ..< leaves out the end, so i takes 0, 1, 2 and 3.

lessons.title: Functions and closures
lessons.summary: Argument labels, defaults, return types and closures.

sections.p: Functions are declared with func; the return type follows ->. Swift callers write each argument's label, so calls read like sentences: share(nuts: 10, among: 5). A parameter can have a label for callers and a different name inside the function, or _ for no label. Parameters can have default values.
A function can return a tuple, a small group of values with names. The caller reads them by name, or takes them apart into separate constants.

A closure is a function without a name, written in braces: { (n: Int) -> Int in n * 3 }. You can keep one in a constant and pass it to other functions. When Swift knows the types, you can drop them, and even the parameter names: $0 is the first argument. A closure that is the last argument can go after the brackets.

practice.why: count defaults to 1. The first parameter has _ so it needs no label, and count does.
The closure after the brackets is f, and $0 is its first argument, 5.

lessons.title: Optionals
lessons.summary: Int?, if let, guard let, ?? and optional chaining.

sections.p: A plain String in Swift always holds a string. When a value may be missing, its type gets a question mark: String? is an optional string, which holds either a string or nil. You can't use an optional as if it were there. if let unwraps it: the body runs only when there is a value, and inside it the name is a plain String.

?? gives a fallback when an optional is nil. ?., optional chaining, goes on only if there is a value: name?.count is the length, or nil. ! forces an optional open and crashes the program if it is nil, so use it rarely.

sections.h: Things that may fail, and guard
sections.p: Many operations return an optional when they may have no answer. Int("42") turns text into a number, or nil if the text isn't one. first(where:) finds the first matching item, or nil. guard let is the other way round from if let: it leaves the function early when the value is missing, and the unwrapped name stays usable for the rest of the function.
sections.out:
42
-1
10 a day
not a number
Found beech

practice.code:
let a: String? = nil
let b: String? = "pine"
print((a?.count ?? 0) + (b?.count ?? 0))
practice.why: a?.count is nil, so ?? gives 0. b?.count is 4. 0 + 4 = 4.
"x" isn't a number, so Int("x") is nil and ?? turns it into 0: 3 + 0 + 5.

practice.q: What does guard let do when the value is nil?
options: Runs its else block, which must leave the function
practice.answer: Runs its else block, which must leave the function
practice.why: guard's else must exit, with return or throw, so after the guard the unwrapped value is always there.

lessons.title: Arrays and dictionaries
lessons.summary: Arrays, dictionaries, sets, and map, filter and reduce.

sections.p: An array is an ordered list of values of one type, written in square brackets. An array made with let can't change; one made with var can be appended to and have items removed. Items are numbered from 0. Printing an array shows strings in quotes.
sections.code:
let trees = ["oak", "ash", "beech"]
print(trees)
print(trees[1])
print(trees.count)
var stash = [3, 5]
stash.append(8)
stash.remove(at: 0)
print(stash)
print(trees.contains("ash"))

sections.p: A dictionary stores values under keys: ["oak": 4]. Looking up a key gives an optional, because the key may not be there. A dictionary has no fixed order, so to print one in a predictable order, go through keys.sorted(). Setting a key to nil removes it.
sections.code:
var stash = ["oak": 4, "hazel": 9]
stash["beech"] = 2
stash["oak", default: 0] += 1
print(stash["pine"] ?? 0)
stash["hazel"] = nil
for tree in stash.keys.sorted() {
    print("\(tree): \(stash[tree]!)")
}

sections.p: Arrays come with functions that take a closure. filter keeps the items that pass a test, map turns each item into something else, and reduce combines them all into one value, starting from the value you give it. sorted, max and joined do what their names say.
sections.code:
let nuts = [4, 11, 7, 2, 9]
print(nuts.filter { $0 > 5 })
print(nuts.map { $0 * 10 })
print(nuts.reduce(0, +))
print(nuts.filter { $0 % 2 == 1 }.reduce(0, +))
print(nuts.max() ?? 0)
let trees = ["beech", "oak", "chestnut"]
print(trees.sorted { $0.count < $1.count })
print(trees.map { $0.uppercased() }.joined(separator: " / "))

practice.why: filter keeps 2, 4 and 6, and map squares each of them.

practice.code:
let ages = ["Hazel": 3, "Acorn": 1]
print(ages["Acorn"] ?? -1)
print(ages["Bob"] ?? -1)
practice.why: A lookup gives an optional. Bob isn't a key, so the lookup is nil and ?? gives -1.

practice.q: What does  let a = [1, 2];  a.append(3)  do?
options: It doesn't compile: a let array can't change
practice.answer: It doesn't compile: a let array can't change
practice.why: An array in a let constant is fixed. Declare it with var to change it.

lessons.title: Structs and classes
lessons.summary: Properties, methods, mutating, and value versus reference types.

sections.p: A struct groups related values and the functions that work on them. Swift writes an initializer for you that takes each property by name. A method that changes the struct's own properties is marked mutating. A computed property works out its value each time it is read.

Structs are value types: assigning one to another name makes a separate copy, so changing the copy leaves the original alone. Classes are reference types: both names point at the same object. Swift code uses structs for most things, and classes when one shared object is really wanted. A class needs its own init.

A protocol lists what a type must provide. Structs, classes and enums can all adopt protocols, and an array of the protocol type can hold any of them. CustomStringConvertible is a built-in protocol: give a type a description and print uses it.
sections.out:
Hazel says chitter
Sage says hoo
Owl called Sage

practice.why: Point is a struct, so q is a separate copy. Changing q leaves p alone.
Counter is a class, so a and b are the same object. Its count is ticked twice.

lessons.title: Enums
lessons.summary: Cases, switch over every case, associated values and raw values.

sections.p: An enum is a type with a fixed list of cases. A switch over an enum must handle every case, so adding a new case makes the compiler point at every switch that misses it. When Swift knows the type, you can write just .autumn. CaseIterable adds allCases, a list of every case.
sections.out:
spring: eat
summer: eat
autumn: bury nuts
winter: dig them up

sections.p: Each case of an enum can carry its own values, called associated values. A switch takes them apart with let. This is a tidy way to say "one of these shapes" or "either a result or a reason it failed".
An enum can give each case a fixed raw value, such as a string or a number. rawValue reads it, and init(rawValue:) goes the other way, giving an optional because the value may match no case.

practice.why: The switch covers both cases of Pet, so no default is needed, and let takes out each case's value.

practice.q: Why does  Tree(rawValue: "Pinus")  give an optional?
options: The raw value might match no case
Enums can't be made from strings
So it can be changed later
practice.answer: The raw value might match no case
practice.why: Any string can be passed in, but only three of them name a tree, so the result is nil for the rest.

lessons.title: Errors, extensions and generics
lessons.summary: throws and do-catch, adding to existing types, type parameters.

sections.p: A function that can fail is marked throws and stops with throw. Any type that adopts the Error protocol can be thrown; an enum is the usual choice. Calls to it must be marked with try, inside a do block whose catch clauses handle each error. try? turns an error into nil instead.
An extension adds methods and computed properties to a type you didn't write, even String or Int. Inside it, self is the value it was used on.

A generic function has a type parameter in angle brackets, <T>, standing for whatever type the caller uses. Arrays and dictionaries are generic too: [String] is short for Array<String>. A constraint like T: Comparable lets the function use < on its values.

practice.why: try? gives nil when the call throws, and ?? swaps nil for "none".
squared is added to Int by the extension, so 3.squared() is 9 and 4.squared() is 16.

lessons.title: Result as a value
lessons.summary: Result success and failure, map, flatMap and get.

sections.p: Result<Success, Failure> is either a .success holding a value or a .failure holding an error. Unlike throw, the failure is a normal return value, so the caller has to look at it. A switch (or get(), which throws the failure) unpacks it. This is the same idea as a carefully written enum with associated values, built into the language.

map transforms a successful value and leaves a failure alone. flatMap chains a second step that itself returns a Result, so failures skip the rest. get() throws the failure, which suits a do/catch or try? when you want an optional again.

guard let can unwrap several optionals at once, and stop early if any is missing. Optional map runs a transform only when there is a value. Together with Result, you choose: missing data stays an optional; a real failure becomes a Result (or a throw).

practice.why: Only the two successes add their values: 2 + 5.
map squares the successful 6; failure would stay a failure.

practice.q: When is Result a better fit than throw?
options: When a failure is a normal outcome the caller should handle as a value
practice.answer: When a failure is a normal outcome the caller should handle as a value
practice.why: Result makes the failure part of the return type, so it can't be ignored by accident.

lessons.title: Pattern matching in depth
lessons.summary: if case, for case, and nested associated values.

sections.p: if case matches one enum case without a full switch, and for case walks a list keeping only the cases you care about. Both can bind associated values with let. Use _ for values you don't need.
sections.out:
first find 8 acorn
gift to Pip
acorn x8, walnut x3

sections.p: One enum's associated value can be another enum. A switch can match both layers at once: .ok(.pair(let a, let b)). That keeps related shapes together without a pile of optional fields.
A case can add a where condition. The branch runs only when the pattern matches and the condition is true. That keeps filters next to the data they care about.

practice.why: for case keeps only the dog cases and binds each name.
The nested pattern matches wrap with inner a(2), and bare matches on its own.

practice.q: What does if case .found(let nut, _) = e do?
options: Runs its body only when e is .found, binding the nut and ignoring the other value
Converts e into a found case
Crashes if e is not found
practice.answer: Runs its body only when e is .found, binding the nut and ignoring the other value
practice.why: if case is a one-case match; _ discards an associated value you don't need.

lessons.title: Project: a nut ledger
lessons.summary: Enums with associated values, a Result-style apply and a report.

sections.p: A ledger is built by replaying a list of events. Each event is one case of an enum with associated values. Applying an event either updates the stock or returns an error string — a tiny result type, without throwing. A gift that asks for more walnuts than you have is skipped and reported; the rest become a sorted table.
sections.out:
skipped: cannot gift 5 walnut: only 3
acorn      5
hazelnut   4
walnut     3
gifts to: Pip

sections.p: Add a traded case that swaps one nut for another and see the compiler point at the unhandled case, keep a history of every stock along the way, or switch ApplyResult for the built-in Result type.

practice.q: Why does apply return ApplyResult instead of throwing?
options: So a bad event can be skipped and reported without stopping the whole replay
Swift cannot throw inside a switch
practice.answer: So a bad event can be skipped and reported without stopping the whole replay
practice.why: Returning an error value keeps the loop in charge, the same idea as Result.
allCases gives both cases in order; acorn is then increased.

practice.q: What does if case .gift(_, _, let to) = e bind?
options: Only the recipient name, when e is a gift
practice.answer: Only the recipient name, when e is a gift
practice.why: The two underscores discard the nut and count; to is bound only for gift events.
